speechtext: There is one question that has not been fully answered by the hon. Minister of Finance. The hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid) makes a statement that this money is being expended in the United States. He lives on the ground, and if that is correct I think the hon. minister should stay his hand until he is perfectly assured that no part of this money is being spent in American territory.

I am so fissured. There are two or three different works going on in that neighbourhood. There is a dam being constructed in connection with the work in that vicinity, and one end of it is upon an American island, and possibly this has led to some confusion. At all events, I am advised that there is no part of this work being done in Ameri-

can territory, and that it is entirely in Canadian territory.

I can prove that a part of it is being done in American territory by correspondence in the department of the lion. Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson). This dam was only proposed to be built within the last two or three years. It never was in the original contract at all.
I know that for a fact, and I Will guarantee to prove it by the correspondence in the Department of Customs. These parties wrote to the Department of Customs and got a statement that the collector at Cardinal need not charge the contractors,duty if they procured a certificate from the Department of Railways and Canals. I make the statement on the floor of this House, and I am prepared to back it up that a portion of this work is In American waters, and that these contractors were relieved from duty on obtaining a certificate from the Department of Railways and Canals. I saw the certificate at the time. I know it was forwarded to Ottawa. I know that the customs offlcer at Cardinal had to get instructions from the Customs Department at Ottawa instructing him that it was all right for him not to collect the duty, because the certificate of the Department of Railways and Canals showed that the work was done in American waters.

I do not think a statement that the contractor submitted that it was in American waters would necessarily prove that we are wrong. I am quite satisfied that the channel is in Canadian waters, and I am bound to act upon that information.

Three-quarters of the work which is being done is in American waters. It is in the form of a large circle around an island. What is called the upper bar is in Canadian waters, while the other part is in American waters, and I know that if the hon. Minister of Customs will look it up, probably about the year 1888, or back there, he will find a certificate from the Department of Railways and Canals, or from the engineers of the department, proving that the work is in American waters. This certificate was' forwarded to Ottawa and the collector got a letter back from the Department of Customs that in view of this certificate, they could not collect duty on the coal used on the dredge while doing the work.
About what year was that ?
During 1888.
But this work was done in 1902.
Yes.

What work does the hon. minister mean ?

That we are now doing in this channel ?

there may be one part on the American side and one part in Canada.

There are three-quarters of it in American waters.

It must be.	This
was done for the purpose of clearing out these rocks that had drifted into the channel, and therefore if they were doing that, certainly part of it was in American waters and part in Canadian waters. I understand from general talk around there that these contractors were supposed to have cleared all this out. But these parties have not hesitated to say that they can handle the government, and they can get a contract to widen the channel, but they do not want anything said about it, believing that they could slide itl through. I am satisfied that the government by doing this work are only going to injure the waters above. It is not necessary.
Could the hon. minister give us any idea as to what the depth of the water is now ?
No, depth of water it not what we desire now. Some blasting had been done, and rocks were left in the channel.
I understand the hon. minister to say that there has been no work done since last year?
That is true.
But the hon. minister told us that there were 17 feet of water.
I am afraid there is not 17 feet of water where these rocks are.

This matter has created so much suspicion that I think the hon. minister should stop the work until he gets a reliable report upon it. The government engineers, it has been proved by Mr. Kennedy, did wrong before, and the hon. Minister of Finance seemed to think that be had a good argument in the report that it was done by friends of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, and that when it was brought to the attention of the minister he stopped it because he could not rely on tlie report of the engineer, and he sent out some oflier engineers to inquire into it. This would seem to be sufficient to arouse such

suspicion in the mind of the hon. Minister of Finance as to cause him to inquire into the situation. In addition to that we have the statement made by an hon. member of this House on his responsibility as a member, by one who lives right in the locality, who has been there all his lifetime and who ought to know the facts. Then, this hon. gentleman's statement is backed up by affidavits and letters from some of the most respectable, the most responsible and the most intelligent men who have been navigating . the St. Lawrence for the last 25 years, many of whom I know personally to be men of integrity and truthfulness, and men who know what they are talking about. If the hon. minister, with all this information in his possession, insists on carryng out this work he will be doing something that will be a scandal and a disgrace to this government.
